etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English banke, from Middle French banque, from Italian banca (“counter, moneychanger's bench or table”), from Lombardic bank (“bench, counter”), from Proto-West Germanic *banki, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz (“bench, counter”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeg- (“to turn, curve, bend, bow”). Doublet of bench, banc, and banco.

definitions.definition: (countable) An institution where one can place and borrow money and take care of financial affairs.

quote.citation: 2013 June 1, “End of the peer show”, in The Economist, volume 407, number 8838, page 71:
quote.text: Finance is seldom romantic. But the idea of peer-to-peer lending comes close. This is an industry that brings together individual savers and lenders on online platforms. […] Banks and credit-card firms are kept out of the picture. Talk to enough people in the field and someone is bound to mention the “democratisation of finance”.

definitions.definition: (countable) A branch office of such an institution.
(countable) An underwriter or controller of a card game.
(countable) A fund from deposits or contributions, to be used in transacting business; a joint stock or capital.

quote.citation: 1625, Francis [Bacon], “Of Usury”, in The Essayes […], 3rd edition, London:  […]  Iohn Haviland for Hanna Barret, →OCLC:
quote.text: Let it be no bank or common stock, but every man be master of his own money.

definitions.definition: (gambling, countable) The sum of money etc. which the dealer or banker has as a fund from which to draw stakes and pay losses.
(slang, uncountable) Money; profit.

quote.text: Military dude was working for a drug dealer, right? and making good bank with it—he was making good money.

definitions.definition: (countable) In certain games, such as dominos, a fund of pieces from which the players are allowed to draw.
(countable, chiefly in combination) A safe and guaranteed place of storage for and retrieval of important items or goods.
(countable) A device used to store coins or currency.
(intransitive) To deal with a bank or financial institution, or for an institution to provide financial services to a client.

quote.citation: 1979, Douglas Adams, The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy:
quote.text: the sort of face you would happily bank with

definitions.definition: (transitive) To put into a bank.
(transitive, slang) To conceal in the rectum for use in prison.
(transitive, finance) To provide banking services to.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English bank, from Old English hōbanca (“couch”) and Old English banc (“bank, hillock, embankment”), from Proto-Germanic *bankô. Akin to Old Norse bakki (“elevation, hill”), Norwegian bakke (“slope, hill”).

definitions.definition: (hydrology) An edge of river, lake, or other watercourse.

quote.citation: 1599 (first performance), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Iulius Cæsar”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i]:
1943 June 8, “Jap Remnants Suffer Heavy Casualties: Alerts In Chungking”, in The Bombay Chronicle‎[1], volume XXXI, number 134, page 1:
quote.text: On the opposite bank of the river other Chinese units attacked Taoshih and Yunmeng north-west of Hankow.

quote.citation: 2014 September 16, Ian Jack, “Is this the end of Britishness”, in The Guardian:
quote.text: Just upstream of Dryburgh Abbey, a reproduction of a classical Greek temple stands at the top of a wooded hillock on the river’s north bank.

definitions.definition: (nautical, hydrology) An elevation under the sea; a shallow area of shifting sand, gravel, mud, and so forth
(geography) A slope of earth, sand, etc.; an embankment.
(aviation) The incline of an aircraft, especially during a turn.
(rail transport) An incline, a hill.

quote.citation: 1940 December, O. S. M. Raw, “The Rhodesia Railways—II”, in Railway Magazine, page 640:
quote.text: This is the hardest duty on the railway, for the trains are heavy and there are some long 1 in 40 banks.

definitions.definition: A mass of clouds.
(mining) The face of the coal at which miners are working.
(mining) A deposit of ore or coal, worked by excavations above water level.
(mining) The ground at the top of a shaft.
(intransitive, aviation) To roll or incline laterally in order to turn.
(transitive) To cause (an aircraft) to bank.
(transitive) To form into a bank or heap, to bank up.
(transitive) To cover the embers of a fire with ashes in order to retain heat.
(transitive) To raise a mound or dike about; to enclose, defend, or fortify with a bank; to embank.

quote.citation: 1601, C[aius] Plinius Secundus [i.e., Pliny the Elder], “(please specify |book=I to XXXVII)”, in Philemon Holland, transl., The Historie of the World. Commonly Called, The Naturall Historie of C. Plinius Secundus. […], (please specify |tome=1 or 2), London:  […]  Adam Islip, →OCLC:
quote.text: Aristoma∣chus would haue them to be stript from their leaues in winter, & in any hand to be banked well about, that the water stand not there in any hollow furrow or hole lower than the other ground

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To pass by the banks of.

quote.citation: c. 1595, William Shakespeare, King John, act 5, scene 2:
quote.text: Have I not heard these islanders shout out / Vive le roi! as I have banked their towns?

definitions.definition: (rail transport, UK) To provide additional power for a train ascending a bank (incline) by attaching another locomotive.

quote.citation: 1942 March, “Notes and News: Locomotive Notes”, in Railway Magazine, page 93:
quote.text: Some interesting facts have recently been made known by the L.N.E.R. concerning the 178-ton Garratt 2-8-0 + 0-8-2 engine No. 2395, which since construction in 1925 has spent the whole of its working life banking coal trains up the 3 miles of 1 in 40 between Wentworth junction and West Silkstone, on the Worsborough branch, near Barnsley.

quote.citation: 1960 July, “Motive Power Miscellany: Western Region”, in Trains Illustrated, page 443:
quote.text: [...] the 4-4-0 unhappily stalled after a stop on Reading Old Bank with its eight-coach load and the Reading Up Line pilot, a "Hall", had to bank the train into Reading General.

quote.citation: 1960 September, P. Ransome-Wallis, “Modern motive power of the German Federal Railway: Part One”, in Trains Ilustrated, page 558:
quote.text: Soon after leaving Bebra the line rises, mostly at 1 in 74, for 7 miles to Cornberg and all trains of over 400 tons are banked.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English bank (“bank”), banke, from Old French banc (“bench”), from Frankish *bank. Akin to Old English benc (“bench”).

definitions.definition: A row or panel of items stored or grouped together.

quote.citation: 2011 December 10, Marc Higginson, “Bolton 1 - 2 Aston Villa”, in BBC Sport‎[2]:
quote.text: Wanderers were finally woken from their slumber when Kevin Davies brought a fine save out of Brad Guzan while, minutes after the restart, Klasnic was blocked out by a bank of Villa defenders.

definitions.definition: A row of keys on a musical keyboard or the equivalent on a typewriter keyboard.
(computing) A contiguous block of memory that is of fixed, hardware-dependent size, but often larger than a page and partitioning the memory such that two distinct banks do not overlap.
(pinball) A set of multiple adjacent drop targets.
(transitive, order and arrangement) To arrange or order in a row.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Probably from French banc. Of Germanic origin, and akin to English bench.

definitions.definition: A bench, as for rowers in a galley; also, a tier of oars.

quote.citation: 1658, Edmund Waller, he Passion of Dido for Æneas:
quote.text: Placed on their banks, the lusty Trojans sweep / Neptune's smooth face, and cleave the yielding deep.

definitions.definition: A bench or seat for judges in court.
The regular term of a court of law, or the full court sitting to hear arguments upon questions of law, as distinguished from a sitting at nisi prius, or a court held for jury trials. See banc[1]
(archaic, printing) A kind of table used by printers.
(music) A bench, or row of keys belonging to a keyboard, as in an organ.[2]
